instantiated_cells.justification: The statute defines lobbying as attempting to influence legislative or administrative action by oral or written communication with covered officials and expressly includes preparation time and appearances at public hearings/meetings or committee service where such preparation or communication occurs.

A “lobbyist” is defined as an individual employed by a principal or who contracts for or receives economic consideration from a principal (other than reimbursement for actual expenses) and whose duties include lobbying on the principal’s behalf.

In the provided lobbying subchapter definitions, no term equivalent to “public entity” is defined (though “agency” and various officials are defined), so the law does not define a generic 'public entity' in this text.

For individuals whose duties are not exclusively lobbying, the statute applies a threshold requiring lobbying communications on at least 5 days within a reporting period, functioning as a materiality/threshold test for lobbyist status.

Lobbying includes attempts to influence 'administrative action' by communicating with an 'agency official,' where agencies are defined as state executive entities and administrative action concerns agency rulemaking.
An 'agency official' includes an agency 'employee or consultant' participating in administrative action, and lobbying covers communications with an agency official.

The definition of 'legislative action' expressly includes the governor’s approval/veto of bills and development of proposals for introduction, bringing the governor’s office within the actions lobbying seeks to influence.

Because 'agency' is broadly defined to include any state board, commission, department, office, council, or committee (excluding legislative councils/committees), communications with officials of such bodies are covered targets for lobbying.
Lobbying is attempting to influence 'legislative action,' which includes actions by the legislature, its houses and committees, and legislators acting in an official capacity.

Lobbying includes communications with a 'legislative employee,' which is defined to include members/officers of the legislature, certain legislative employees, and employees of legislative service agencies.
Lobbying is defined as communications with any 'elective state official,' a category of elected officials defined in the statute.
Covered lobbying targets include 'agency officials' and 'legislative employees,' both of which include employees (and consultants) of public bodies participating in official actions.
The provided definitions do not define a 'public entity' at all, and therefore do not rely on any charter-based criteria.
Because no 'public entity' definition appears in the provided statutory text, there is no ownership-based test specified for such an entity.
The statute text provided contains no definition of 'public entity' and thus includes no revenue-structure criterion for defining one.
